title: Chapter 50 – Cheng Yun's Question
html:
[Sect Outer Court – Inspector Cheng Yun]

Cheng Yun has been an inspector for nineteen years, and in that time he has learned that the most dangerous number in any ledger is the one that is slightly too good.

He reads it in the saddle. It is the second week of summer, hot and bright, and the road up to Green Pine Hill is a ribbon of white dust between fields of young millet. His horse is a stolid gray gelding, bought at the Outer Court's expense and ridden at his own. The ledger is a thin one, copied by his clerk from the Willow Ford market rolls. He turns a page with a thumb, and the tiny characters pass under his eye in neat gray columns.

Spirit-iron, nineteen dozen. Heartleaf salve, forty-one jars. Marrow Wash, six dozen. Blood Seal, four.

Four dozen, in a month. From a clan that sold three dozen of anything, the whole of last year.

He closes the book. The gelding picks its way round a pothole. On either side of the road the millet stirs in a faint breeze, and the sun is warm on his neck, and a thin brown lark is going up and up into the white sky.

It is a very nice morning, he thinks. It is the sort of morning on which a man might make a mistake.

He is thirty-eight years old. He is a lean, sallow man in a gray traveling robe, with the thin long hands of a scribe and a mouth that gives nothing away. He is an early Foundation cultivator, which is a good deal more than the Outer Court deserves from an inspector of provincial clans, and he has been in the post nineteen years because he has declined, three times, to be promoted out of it. He likes the work. He likes it as a man likes a long, quiet, dry puzzle. A clan is a ledger with people in it, and every ledger, if one reads it patiently, will tell the truth about the people.

He has been reading Green Pine's for a year. He has never in his life been so interested.

* * *

The Patriarch receives him in the study, which is the same small tidy room he remembers, with the same faint smell of ink and old paper. There is tea. There are three kinds of cake, one of them honey, which he does not remember being offered in the spring. The Patriarch is standing when he comes in, and bows, correctly, a little deeper than the rank demands. He looks well.

Too well. Cheng Yun notes it, as he notes everything, without moving his face.

In the spring, Lin Wenyuan was a gray, hollow, careful man, with the exhausted stillness of one who has been up all night too many nights. He is not that man now. His color is good. His movements are easy. He carries himself like someone whose bones have recently stopped hurting.

"Inspector," says Wenyuan. "You are most welcome. I hope the road was kind."

"It was dusty. But the millet is fine." Cheng Yun sits. "I see the hill has been busy."

"We have been working."

"So I gather." He takes the ledger from his sleeve and lays it on the table. He does not open it. "I will be plain, Patriarch, since I think it is a courtesy. You have a hill that is losing its vein at three parts in a hundred, and has been for a decade. The vein fell by a further eight percent in the last quarter, I understand, according to your own stele. Your upper terraces are cold. Your rice is poor. Your tribute is due in the autumn, and in the spring you were forty stones short." He pauses. "And in the last four months your treasury has grown by four hundred."

"Yes."

"I should like to know why."

The Patriarch folds his hands on the desk.

It is a thing Cheng Yun has seen many times in many studies. The moment before a man decides what kind of liar he is. It is brief, and quiet, and in some men it is a flinch. In Lin Wenyuan it is not. It is a sort of settling, like a bird folding its wings, and the dark eyes come up and meet his, calm and steady and rather tired.

"Because we hired a master," says Wenyuan.

* * *

They go to see him at noon.

The granary has changed. It is a long, low, whitewashed building with a high roof, and it stands, now, on a neat gravel apron, with a stream-fed trough along one wall and a rack of drying slag on the other. A thin plume of gray smoke goes up from the chimney. The smell is clean and hot and mineral, the smell of a forge that is looked after. A young man in a leather apron nods to them from the door, and a boy of twelve runs past with a bucket.

And inside, in the long dim hall, under the roof, an old man is standing at a furnace.

He is bent. That is the first thing. He is bent like a shepherd's crook, round-shouldered and stoop-necked, with a thick gray beard and a face the color of a smoked ham. He has one arm. The other sleeve is pinned up neatly at the elbow. In his remaining hand he holds a long iron rod, bent at the tip, and with it he is turning a crucible of white-hot metal in the heart of the fire, slowly, patiently, as a man turns a child in a cradle.

He does not look up.

"Hu," says the Patriarch, quietly. "This is Inspector Cheng Yun, of the Outer Court."

"I know who it is," says the old man. He does not turn. His voice is a dry rasp. "I have known since he came down the road. He rides a gelding with a bad off-hind. He has a very light seat. A man who sits his horse like that has done a great deal of walking, and does not trust anything that cannot be put down." The rod turns. "Sit, Inspector. There is a stool. Do not touch the trough."

Cheng Yun sits.

He has expected a great many things. He had expected a drunk. The whole of Green Pine knows that Old Hu of the granary was a famous drunkard, the clan's chief embarrassment, a sort of local legend, a man who had once been an artisan of the Sect and had come down, through some sorry story, to dying slowly in a forgotten shed. He had not expected this. He had not expected the white-hot steady glow, and the practiced economical turn of the rod, and the absolute quiet in the great room, like a church.

He is a master, he thinks. Whatever else he is, he is that.

"I hear," says Cheng Yun, "that you make spirit-iron out of slag."

"I make it out of what is put in front of me."

"The Sect's own refiners say it cannot be done. The yield is too low."

"The Sect's refiners are afraid of the heat." A dry little cough. "I am not."

"Mm." Cheng Yun watches the crucible. It is a most beautiful color. It is the color of the heart of a flower. "It is a very singular gift. I wonder that nobody found it before."

"Someone did," says Hu. He lifts the rod. A long thin thread of glowing metal pours from the crucible into a clay mold, with a hiss like a drawn breath, and a puff of white steam rolls up under the rafters. "He is dead."

He sets the rod down, at last, and turns.

Cheng Yun has seen the old man's face before, once, years ago, in a portrait. He cannot at first recall where. The gray beard has changed it, and the stoop, and the cloud on one eye. But the other eye is very clear, and very dark, and very steady, and it meets his without a flicker.

Sha Hu, thinks Cheng Yun, with something very like awe. The Veiled Forge. He had thought the man dead twenty years.

He says nothing. He does not move his face.

"The Inspector is welcome to examine the work," says Hu, quietly. "The ingots, the books, my fees. I have a list. Nothing is hidden." The clear eye holds his. "I ask only that he not ask me to be a better man than I am."

"I would not dream of it," says Cheng Yun.

He means it.

* * *

He does not find the thing he is looking for in the granary.

He walks the whole afternoon. The treasury, with its neat brown strongboxes. The market receipts, which are in perfect order. The guardhouse, where a big gaunt man with a splinted arm is drilling a dozen young men in the yard, and stops, mid-stroke, and bows. The schoolhouse, where an old teacher is reading aloud from the Founder's Precepts to a room full of seven-year-olds. The herb garden, where a stout woman in a straw hat shows him a bed of pale blue flowers, frostbell and mourner's cup, and says with perfect composure that they are a thing the clan has begun to grow, in the lower terraces, since the Matron's second wife brought the cuttings from the south.

All of it is in order. All of it is plausible. All of it is, he reflects, rather too well prepared.

A man who has nothing to hide does not clean the shelf before the guest arrives.

He had thought, when he came, that the money would be the thread. He had expected to find some quiet smuggling, a hill-clan's small, forgivable sin: a vein of ore hidden in the north quarry, or a secret contract with a Ford merchant, or a sell-off of the Founder's treasure. It would have been a delicate matter. He would have had to decide how much he wished to know.

But it is not that. It is something he cannot see. It is like a note in a piece of music that is just a quarter-tone off. The numbers add. The faces smile. And at the back of every room, in the corner of every eye, there is a small, dry, shared tension, like a cord that has been drawn tight and not yet cut.

They are afraid, he thinks. Not of me. Of something. And they have been afraid for a while.

It is almost dusk when he comes, by himself, to the north slope, where the old quarry lies.

* * *

It is a pleasant place, in the evening. The great gray bowl of the quarry is full of warm light and swallows. The spoil heaps, once heaped with black slag, are lower now, scoured and neat. A thin stream runs down the east side. At the foot of the east wall, where the cut stone has been stepped away in great shelves, he stops.

He does not know why.

It is the sort of thing a man cannot explain. He has been walking, with his hands in his sleeves, looking at nothing in particular. And then something has made him stop. Some small cold prickle on the back of the neck, some faint shift in the air. He stands very still. A swallow darts past his ear. The light slants down the quarry wall, gold, and the shadow at its foot is blue.

He holds out his hand.

It is a gesture he has made a thousand times, a gentle forward turn of the palm, to feel what a place remembers. He does not use Qi. He does not need to. A man with a Foundation does not so much sense as hear, in the long soft ways of the air.

And the air at the foot of the east wall is cold.

It is not the cold of shadow. It is thin and dry and strange, like the breath of a cellar, and it comes in a narrow vertical line, from the height of his knee to above his head, as if someone had very recently drawn a knife through the world and sewn it shut. He knows the feel of it. He has felt it only once before, in the spring, in the quick pale flicker of a young pangolin's shell.

Seam, thinks Cheng Yun.

The word is dry as dust. He turns it over, once, twice, with great care, as a man turns over a snake.

A seamwalker has been here. Not once. A great many times. The edges are worn. He puts out one finger and does not quite touch the air. And it has been opened, in the last month, by something larger than the beast.

"Inspector."

He does not start. He has been expecting it, in the part of himself that never stops listening, for some little while.

"Young master," he says.

* * *

The boy is standing on the lip of the quarry above him, in the long gold light, with his hands at his sides.

He is not much to look at. He is, as the file says, ten years old, thin, dark, quiet, with a mop of straight black hair and a gray robe a little too short in the sleeve. He holds himself very still. He has, Cheng Yun notes, grown since the spring, a hand's breadth at least. And in the full light, at the edge of the dark pupils, there is something faint. A ring. Pale. A thread of gold.

That is not a feature of a second-stage, he thinks.

"I did not know anyone was here," says Jian. "I am sorry. I came to check the wires."

"The wires?"

"For the rabbits." The boy comes down the shelf, lightly, one step and another. He does not look at the foot of the wall. He does not look at anything. "They get into the spoil. Hu says they gnaw the pegs."

"Ah." Cheng Yun tilts his head. "I had not thought rabbits were a problem for a smith."

"They are, if you do not watch them."

It is, of course, perfectly true, and perfectly meaningless. Cheng Yun regards him with a small dry interest. It is an expression he has worn for nineteen years, and has found useful in the presence of lies. A child's lie is clumsy, and a master's lie is smooth. This is neither. It is an utterly flat statement of a fact that is not the fact, delivered with the plain trust of someone who has no need to be believed.

It is the best I have ever seen, he thinks. From a boy.

"I had meant to ask you something," says Cheng Yun.

"Yes, sir."

"When I was last here, in the spring, a registrar's jade read your cultivation at the second stage. Your cousin Lin Feng, whom I have in the Outer Court now, tells me in his letters that it is a most remarkable second stage. A second stage that can hold a Mirror Guard for fifty-eight breaths." He smiles. "I find I should like to meet it."

The boy looks at him, steadily. His expression does not change.

"It is not remarkable," he says. "I have a good teacher."

"Hu?"

"And my mother."

"Of course." The inspector lets a small silence fall. The swallows are circling. Far below in the valley a dog barks, and a cow lows, and the evening smoke of four hundred hearths is beginning to rise. "You will, I hope, forgive an old man's curiosity. I have been looking at your hill for a year. I have not found what I am looking for. And I find, standing here, with the light going, that I am not entirely sure it is a thing a man could find."

"No, sir."

"No?"

"It is not a thing," says Jian. "It is a house. It has a great many rooms." He is quite grave. "The Inspector is welcome in all of them. Except the ones that are somebody's bedroom."

It is a very small joke. It is not a joke at all. Cheng Yun finds, to his astonishment, that he has laughed.

* * *

He has supper with the Patriarch, because it would be an insult not to.

It is a plain meal in the Patriarch's own room: millet, a river fish, pickled greens, a flask of the clan's thin yellow wine. His wife serves. She is a quiet woman in gray, with the straight back and the watchful hands of someone who has been, in her time, a great deal more than she says. She sets down the dishes without a word, and when she has gone, Wenyuan pours.

"I will not ask you to forgive the cake," he says. "My Aunt makes it when she is nervous."

"It was very good." Cheng Yun sips. "Patriarch, I think I may speak frankly. I think you would like me to."

"I should like it very much."

"You hired a master." He sets down the cup. "A one-armed drunk whom the whole hill has known for ten years. He sits in a granary, with a forge that did not exist in the spring, and turns out a quality of iron that I have not seen outside the Sect's own vaults. Between you and me, Lin Wenyuan, that is the truth, and it is not the whole of the truth. I do not ask for the rest. I ask only that you should know I have seen the shape of it."

Wenyuan does not move.

"I have watched this clan for a year," says Cheng Yun, "and I have formed an opinion. It is a thing I should not do. An inspector ought to be a mirror. But I have found, to my annoyance, that I like you. I like your son. I like the old man in the granary, who is clearly something much more than he says, and I like his courtesy in not asking me to look at it." He sighs. "I have been nineteen years in this post. I have never liked anyone."

"You flatter us."

"I do nothing of the kind. I am simply warning you." The thin sallow face is quite still. "Shen Wuye will read my report in three weeks. I intend to delay it thirty days. I have some small standing, and he will let me. After that I shall have to write it. And what I write will be the truth, as far as it is a thing I know."

"I understand."

"You do not. Not yet." He leans forward. "There are three men, Patriarch, who want what you have. I do not know what it is. I have not asked. I know only that Zhao Bei, the steward of Red Ridge, has been sending his clerks to the Ford every ninth day for a month, to count the carts. He has four hundred men. He is a patient man, and a greedy one, and he has a Patriarch behind him who has not forgiven the spring."

"Zhao Heng."

"Yes. Who is, I hear, a good deal more hurt than he lets the world see. A man like that does not forgive. He waits." Cheng Yun picks up his cup. "And then there is the Blood Shadow. Which I would rather not discuss."

"We have had some acquaintance."

"I gathered. I found the ash of two Drips, on the northern slope, in the spring." A small, dry pause. "I did not write that down either."

Wenyuan looks at him for a long moment. Then, slowly, he begins to smile.

"Inspector," he says. "May I pour you another cup?"

"I should be glad of it."

They drink, in a silence that is neither easy nor uneasy, but is, in its way, a kind of understanding. Outside, the wind has risen, and the great pines on the ridge are sighing like a distant sea. In the next room, very faintly, a child is humming over a game of counters, and a small scaled thing scratches at the door.

"One thing more," says Cheng Yun, at the end. He rises. "If you should wish to send a letter, Patriarch, to the Arbiter, in a hurry, without a three-week delay, you may give it to me. I ride back through the Ford on the fourth. It will reach him in three days." He bows, a very little. "I do not suggest what it should say."

"I will think on it."

"Do."

* * *

He does not write the report that night.

He sits in the guest room of the hall, a plain clean room with a narrow bed and a window that looks west over the terraces, and he lights a lamp, and takes out brush and ink. Below the window, in the yard, a few of the guards are playing dice by lantern light. The air smells of wood smoke and mown grass. He sets the paper straight on the table. He dips the brush.

To the Arbiter of the Outer Court, Shen Wuye. Report of the Inspector Cheng Yun, concerning the audit of the Lin clan of Green Pine Hill. Second visit.

He writes four lines. He crosses them out.

It is a good clan, he thinks. It is a poor clan with a Patriarch who tells the truth and a smith who tells the truth and a boy who, I think, has never once in his life been wholly honest and has never told a lie that mattered. He sets down the brush. And it is a clan with a thing in the quarry that I do not understand, and that I think the Blood Shadow wants, and that Red Ridge wants, and that the boy has been paying for, with something I cannot name, for some while.

If I write that, Shen will read it in three weeks and send a squad.

And the squad will take the hill.

He sits very still.

He is not a sentimental man. He has stood on a great many hillsides, and watched a great many clans go under, and written a great many entries in a great many ledgers, and he has never once let a feeling stand between him and the truth. It is the whole of his craft. It is the one thing he has that the Outer Court cannot buy.

But he finds, tonight, that there are two truths. There is the one that goes in the ledger. And there is the one he saw in the quarry, in the long gold light, in the face of a ten-year-old who laughed.

Thirty days, he thinks. I shall hold the report thirty days.

He takes a fresh sheet. He writes, in a clear fine hand, three lines to the Arbiter, to say that the audit is not yet complete, that the clan's accounts are in order, that the Inspector requires a further month to examine the question of the vein. He seals it. He sets it by the lamp.

Then he takes out a second sheet, a plain one, and writes three words on it, and holds it to the flame.

Hu. Sha Hu.

It curls, and blackens, and drops to the sill in a small gray flake. And Cheng Yun sits on in the quiet, with the lamp burning low, and the dice rattling in the yard below, and the wind stirring the pines on the hill. He does not sleep for a long time. He is thinking about the first thing the boy said to him, in the quarry, with the light behind him.

I came to check the wires.

A boy who counts, he thinks. And who checks his wires.

It is, as far as he knows, the first time in nineteen years that he has failed to finish a report.
